implementation_notes: pygame ships the driver: Clock.tick(framerate) 'should be called once per frame. It will compute how many milliseconds have passed since the previous call' and, when given a framerate, 'will delay to keep the game running slower than the given ticks per second'; get_time() returns the ms between the last two tick calls, get_rawtime() the same without the deliberate delay, and get_fps() averages the last ten calls. What replaces the classic structure: Clock.tick both paces the loop and measures frame time - the delay half of a hand-written loop plus the clock read - leaving only the accumulator for a fixed-step simulation, while the event pump (pygame.event.get()) is the non-blocking input drain. The docs are explicit about the trade: tick uses SDL_Delay and 'is not accurate on every platform, but does not use much CPU. Use tick_busy_loop if you want an accurate timer, and don't mind chewing CPU'.
code_sketch:
clock = pygame.time.Clock()
DT = 1 / 60
lag = 0.0
while running:
    for event in pygame.event.get():        # never blocks
        running &= event.type != pygame.QUIT
    lag = min(lag + clock.tick(60) / 1000, 0.25)   # tick paces + measures
    while lag >= DT:
        step(DT)                             # fixed-step simulation
        lag -= DT
    draw(lag / DT)                           # interpolate
    pygame.display.flip()
pitfalls: Clock.tick(framerate) makes get_time() include its own sleeping; use get_rawtime() when the simulation needs the real processing time of the frame.

The module warns most platforms have a timer resolution around 10 milliseconds, so 60 FPS pacing is approximate; derive simulation deltas from the returned milliseconds, not from the requested framerate.
tick_busy_loop trades CPU for accuracy, and a busy Python loop holds the GIL, starving threads that share the interpreter.
Blocking work inside the loop (network, file I/O, time.sleep) stops the world; queue it off-loop.

variants.name: Hand-written perf_counter loop (headless)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a framework, the time module is enough: perf_counter() returns 'the value (in fractional seconds) of a performance counter, i.e. a clock with the highest available resolution to measure a short duration', includes time elapsed during sleep, and only differences between two calls are meaningful. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - a while loop reads perf_counter twice, accumulates the delta with a clamp, steps fixed dt and paces with time.sleep, which accepts fractional seconds. This is the shape for headless simulations, tick-based servers and tests, and it is where the interpreter's GIL matters, because a loop that never sleeps starves other Python threads.
variants.idiom_name: time.perf_counter() delta accumulator with time.sleep() pacing
variants.code_sketch:
DT = 1 / 60
prev = time.perf_counter()
lag = 0.0
while running:
    now = time.perf_counter()
    lag += now - prev; prev = now           # monotonic, high-resolution
    lag = min(lag, 0.25)                    # clamp: no spiral of death
    drain_input()
    while lag >= DT:
        step(DT); lag -= DT
    render(lag / DT)
    time.sleep(max(0.0, DT / 2))            # coarse pacing; re-measured above
pitfalls: time.time() is wall-clock and can jump (NTP or manual changes); only perf_counter()/monotonic() differences are safe for the loop.
time.sleep may sleep longer than requested; never treat the requested interval as the elapsed time.
A tight loop holds the GIL and starves other threads; add a sleep or hand work to a worker process when the loop must stay responsive.
Precision is platform-dependent and CPython ties perf_counter to the monotonic clock (the same clock since 3.13); mixing it with time.time() readings breaks interval arithmetic.
